title: Error recovery: define fd state after failed operations
description:
The behavior of an operation fd after an error is unspecified. Developers will encounter errors and not know whether the fd is still usable.

Unspecified cases:
1. write() returns an error (copy_from_user failure, ops->update() failure, outbuf full). Is the fd still usable? Can the caller retry the write? Is the accumulated output discarded?
2. read() returns -EBADMSG (GCM tag verification failure). Is the fd dead? Can the caller try again with a different tag via SET_TAG + write() + read()?
3. ops->finalize() returns an error. Same question.
4. CRYPTO2DEV_IOC_FINALIZE returns an error. Same question.

HUMAN DECISION NEEDED:

Error recovery model — two options:

A. 'Fd is dead on any error': any error from write(), read(), or FINALIZE puts the fd in an error state. Subsequent write()/read() return -EIO until RESET is called. Clean and predictable. Forces explicit recovery.

B. 'Soft errors are retryable': copy_from_user failures (transient) leave the fd in its prior state — nothing was consumed. wolfCrypt errors (bad key, bad padding) are fatal to the session — fd requires RESET. Distinguishes kernel errors from crypto errors.

C. 'Only fatal for finalization errors': errors during update() are retryable (nothing committed); errors during finalize() are fatal (session state is indeterminate).

Recommendation: A is safest and easiest to specify. Implement a per-fd error flag; RESET clears it.

Work items once decision is made:
- Add error state tracking to crypto2dev_fd_state
- Implement RESET clearing the error state
- Document all error return paths and their effect on fd state in a state machine comment in crypto2dev_fd.c
- Add test cases: verify write() after update() error returns correct code; verify RESET restores usability
notes: DECISION 2026-04-17: Option A + -EFAULT carve-out. Any error that reaches update() or finalize() marks the session dead (state->error=true); subsequent write()/read() return -EIO until RESET. copy_from_user failure in write() returns early before lock/state-touch (already safe). copy_to_user failure in read() leaves data in outbuf — caller can retry with valid pointer (already safe). RESET clears the error flag.
